newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: TSUMEB GUARDS WITHOUT FOOD, MANAGER FREE.
newsitem.headline: TSUMEB GUARDS WITHOUT FOOD, MANAGER FREE.

text.p: Security staff trapped by striking miners at Namibia's Tsumeb Corp Ltd (TCL) have now gone three days without food, but a mine-manager blockaded in his own home has been freed, mine-owners Goldfields of Namibia said on Thursday.

The guards, numbering up to 30, ate their last meal on Monday. Armed strikers from the Mineworkers' Union of Namibia (MUN) have surrounded them at the copper mine, saying they can leave, but only if they submit a list of their names.
The guards have refused and the firm is also unwilling to withdraw them, and their dogs, from the site as that would surrender it totally into the hands of the strikers.
"We have not had any luck getting food to them," a Goldfields spokesman told Reuters by phone from Namibia.
However, mine manager Tony de Beer has now been allowed free access to and from his house after spending two days there trapped with his wife.
"Tony has been able to get around today," he said, though he added armed men were still standing outside his property.
The six week old wages strike has become increasingly bitter and exploded into crisis this week after MUN members took control of the group's three mines -- Otjihase, Kombat and Tsumeb.
Efforts by Namibian government ministers on Wednesday failed to persuade the strikers to put down their weapons, which include shot-guns and pangas (large knives).
The strikers still control all three mines.
"Nothing has changed since yesterday (Wednesday). The atmosphere is still very tense," the spokesman said.

The strike over pay began with TCL offering a seven percent rise and the union demanding 14.5 percent. The firm hopes to table a new pay offer on Friday aimed at settling the dispute or, at least, starting mediation again.
Tsumeb mines and smelters have been shut down since August 23. The strike is costing TCL some 80 tonnes a day in lost copper production and a similar amount in lost lead.
